claims.text: The simultaneous high strength and ductility of high-entropy alloys arise from severe lattice distortion caused by a multi-element random solid-solution structure.
Severe lattice distortion impedes dislocation motion.
The random solid-solution structure promotes dislocation storage and multiplication under stress.
The proposed comparison concerns fully annealed, single-phase HEAs and conventional single-element or binary alloys of similar crystal structure.
Dynamic tensile or compression loading over varying strain rates can reveal the proposed difference between the HEA and baseline.
The hypothesis is intended to apply from room temperature to moderate temperatures and from approximately 10^-4 to 10^2 s^-1.
Severe lattice distortion and local chemical complexity are the structural mediators in the HEA matrix.
Lattice distortion increases the energy barrier for dislocation motion.
An increased barrier to dislocation motion produces higher yield strength.
The random atomic environment facilitates dislocation storage and multiplication.
Enhanced dislocation storage and multiplication increase strain hardening and ductility under dynamic loading.
HEAs will have higher yield strength than the baseline alloy under dynamic loading.
HEAs will have greater uniform elongation than the baseline alloy under dynamic loading.
The HEA–baseline mechanical-property difference will be greatest at intermediate strain rates.
The baseline alloy should have a crystal structure and grain size similar to those of the HEA.
The hypothesis may not hold for multiphase HEAs.
The hypothesis may not hold at very high strain rates because other mechanisms may dominate.
